JavaScript. tsc emits .js and deletes the types.

It only runs if you keep the .ts extension in the browser.

questions.question: Which annotation compiles for a string binding?
options: let name: String = "Ada"; is the usual form; lowercase string is the wrapper.
let name: string? = "Ada"; the ? goes after the type name.
let name: string = "Ada";
let name: str = "Ada"; str is the primitive alias.
questions.explanation: TypeScript annotations use a colon and lowercase primitives. String is the wrapper object type.

questions.question: After tsc, which is the emitted JavaScript?
options: function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; }
function add(a, b): number { return a + b; }
The compiler refuses to emit because types must remain.
questions.explanation: Code generation is independent of types. Annotations are deleted. The JS still adds two values.

options: any, because there is no annotation.
number
The literal 42, because let keeps literals.
unknown, the default for unannotated lets.
questions.explanation: let n = 42 infers number. const n = 42 infers the literal 42.

questions.question: What does `as string` do here?
options: It converts raw to a string at runtime, like String(raw).
It is a type assertion: it tells the checker to treat raw as string without converting.
It is the same as annotating const name: string = raw when raw is unknown.
It throws if raw is not a string.
questions.explanation: Assertions do not convert. Prefer an annotation or a real runtime check.

questions.question: Which top type still requires a check before you call .toUpperCase()?
options: any — you must narrow any before calling methods.
unknown — you must narrow it first.
never — it has every method.
void — it is a string alias.
questions.explanation: unknown is the safe top type. any disables checking. never is the empty type.

questions.question: What does void mean on a function type?
options: The function does not return at all; it always throws.
Callers should ignore the return value.
The function returns null.
The function returns never.
questions.explanation: void means ignore the return. never means the function does not complete normally.

questions.question: Why can tsc still emit JavaScript when there is a type error?
options: It cannot. Type errors always block emit.
Code generation is independent of the type system unless you set noEmitOnError.
Because types are still present at runtime and get repaired there.
Because tsc rewrites the assignment to Number("hi").
questions.explanation: Type checking and emit are separate. A program with type errors can still produce JS.
